failure.message: The visual review found 3 serious problems with how the scene is drawn or computed. You have not been charged. It was corrected automatically once, but it still did not pass. Revise plan prepares a simpler plan from your request for you to review, using up to 56 AI credits; nothing is built until you press Generate.

plan.title: Why a too-large learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
plan.description: A ball sits on a long, narrow bowl-shaped loss surface. Each step, it moves downhill by the learning rate times the slope, leaving a trail. An arrow shows the step it is about to take. With a small learning rate the ball slides into the bottom. As you raise it, the ball starts zigzagging across the steep sides of the narrow valley. Past a clear tipping point, every jump overshoots by more than the last, and the ball climbs up and off the bowl.
plan.reason: You can find the tipping point yourself by changing the learning rate and watching the same descent shrink toward the bottom, bounce forever, or blow up. A readout shows the number that decides which one happens.
interactions: Step the descent one move at a time or let it play, and pause at any point.
Change the learning rate. At the default steepness the ball settles below 0.5, bounces forever at exactly 0.5, and grows each step until it leaves the surface above 0.5.
Change the steepness of the narrow direction. The tipping point moves to 2 divided by the steepness, so a steeper valley blows up at a smaller learning rate.
Use 'Restart descent' to send the ball back to its start and clear its trail while keeping your current settings.
Orbit the camera to view the zigzag from above or from the side.
assumptions: This is an illustration: a made-up bowl-shaped loss surface, not a real model's loss.
The loss is 0.5 × (x² + steepness × y²). It curves gently along one direction (curvature 1) and more sharply along the other (curvature = steepness).
Each step is plain gradient descent: new position = old position − learning rate × slope, with no momentum and no noise.

Each step multiplies the distance to the bottom in each direction by (1 − learning rate × curvature); a readout shows this factor for the steep direction. Size below 1: it shrinks. Exactly 1: it bounces forever. Above 1: it grows. Exact here; only approximate near a real network's minimum.
The ball starts at the same fixed point every time, away from the bottom along both directions.
The arrow shows the step about to be taken: the downhill direction (opposite the slope), scaled by the learning rate.
limitations: The run stops after 40 steps, when the loss drops below 0.001 (labelled 'converged'), or when the ball leaves the edge of the drawn surface (labelled 'diverged'). After that the loss would keep growing without limit, but it is not drawn.
Real loss surfaces are not perfect bowls, so in practice the tipping point is only roughly 2 divided by the sharpest curvature, and that curvature can change during training.
plan.learningGoal: Gradient descent diverges when the learning rate times the steepest curvature is above 2. Each step then overshoots the bottom by more than it started away, so the error grows instead of shrinking.

draft.title: Why a too-large learning rate makes gradient descent blow up
draft.description: A blue bowl-shaped loss surface, long along x and narrow along z, seen from above at an angle so the floor is visible. A red ball starts on one end. Each step it moves by minus the learning rate times the slope, leaving an orange trail; an orange arrow shows the next step. Small learning rates slide the ball to the bottom. Larger ones zigzag across the narrow valley. When learning rate × steepness is above 2, each zigzag gets bigger and the ball leaves the surface. Readouts show the status, the steep-direction factor, the tipping point, the loss and the steps taken.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up bowl-shaped loss surface, not a real model's loss.
Loss = 0.5 × (x² + steepness × z²): curvature 1 along x, curvature = steepness along z. The surface is drawn at 0.4 × loss; changing steepness narrows it along z.
Each step: new position = old − learning rate × slope, no momentum or noise. The arrow is the next step at its true length (scale 1), pointing downhill.

Each step multiplies the z distance by (1 − learning rate × steepness), shown in a readout. Size below 1 shrinks, exactly 1 bounces forever, above 1 grows. Exact here; only approximate near a real minimum.

The ball starts at x = −2.6, z = 0.8. The run stops after 40 steps (stopped), when loss < 0.001 (converged), or when the ball leaves the drawn surface (diverged). Past the rim the ball is drawn at the rim height; the loss readout stays true.
Changing the learning rate starts a new descent and keeps the last path as a faint ghost for comparison; changing steepness or Restart descent clears both paths.

From camera [4.5,6.5,6.5], the line of sight to (0,0,0) passes under the surface near z=1.5. Lower or swing the camera (or raise the target) so the floor and the minimum can be seen.

The 'Status' text readout (paused/running/converged/diverged/stopped) is missing from the readout line, which shows only the factor, tipping point, loss and steps. The plan promises the run ends labelled 'converged' or 'diverged', but the learner never sees that label.

At lr 0.14, after 14 steps (loss 0.050), the red ball is hidden in the default view: the front wall of the bowl blocks it.
